l: Toser's water system, Travels in Morocco
s: is_supplied_by Wad Meshra An abundant spring called Meshra rises at a small rocky mountain northwest of Toser. It runs along the city walls, divides into three branches, waters Toser’s gardens and neighboring villages, and eventually disappears into the sand; the town’s wells are insufficient, so inhabitants fetch water from Wad Meshra.

Sheikh Tahid, the leading man at Toser, collects the Jereed’s tribute for the Bey. When he fails to have it ready, the Bey imprisons, bastinadoes, and chains him while searches find no money. His gardens are sold for 15,000 piastres and his wife adds 1,000, securing his release.

l: tribute of the Jereed, Travels in Morocco
s: The tribute is a yearly levy collected by a Sheikh, who gathers dates from the people and pays the Bey a fixed sum on arrival. At Toser it is assessed at two bunches for each date-tree; those unable to provide it face imprisonment and punishment. It includes 500 camel-loads of dates from Toser, Nefta, and surrounding districts, plus money and woollen goods, totaling 529 loads and an estimated £9,110, excluding smaller animal presents.

The loted is a deer-like animal about the size of a fallow deer, with a deer-like head whose eye sits farther up. The female lacks a goat-like beard and has long hair from head to chest and over the fore-legs. Sheikh Ali brought in a female and young one he had shot.
Sahara mirage is the repeated appearance of water on salt-covered or sandy surfaces, causing travelers to see shores, bays, and islands before recognizing a salt plain with sand heaps, not a lake.
Ghabs is a place with better-built towns, a water-filled river, fertile soil, and dates inferior to those of the Jereed; Santa Maria arrives safely after a lonely journey.
Sultan Kaed, a Hammama chief, became one of its greatest leaders, distinguished himself in fighting against the French before Constantina, and died at an extremely old age.

l: sale of Sheikh Tahib's gardens, Travels in Morocco
s: Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres; his wife added 1,000 piastres, and Sheikh Tahib was set at liberty.
The date harvest comes in considerable quantity but not great abundance, including esteemed Degalah; superior ripeness is attributed to only one day of rain in the Jereed during the past year.

include lascivious actions [performed by men and women as indispensable entertainment] On Moorish feastdays, masked men performed lascivious and indecent actions, sometimes dressing as women and dancing indecently. Such actions were described as an indispensable part of the entertainment.

l: death of Sultan Kaed, Travels in Morocco
s: is_a death Sultan Kaed, one of the greatest chiefs of the Hammama, died. He was extremely old, and the text remarks that people live to a good old age in the burning climate.
Moorish authorities at Rabat held high duties and commerce monopolies, detained European residents during danger, then fled or failed to prevent the city's destruction.

l: Europeans of Mogador, Travels in Morocco
s: are_exposed_to Mogador sack and destruction [during the bombardment and sack] The British Consul, his wife, Mr. and Mrs. Robertson, and other Europeans were detained in Mogador during the bombardment. Several escaped through the violence of the sack, aided by Mr. Lucas and others, while some residents were left behind.

Railways are proposed for Tunis, alongside water ducts, to distribute water and transport it from Zazwan to the Jereed. The text notes French discussion of an Algiers–Blidah line and argues developed Tunisian resources could make railways profitable.

originates_at Zazwan [the best and most delicious water in the Regency] The party found bad, salty water at Sheesheeah, brought from some distance. Ancient aqueducts and water-regulating structures were seen at Byrlafee and Gilma, and the text proposes using railway lines and ducts to carry good water from Zazwan to the dry deserts of the Jereed.

l: return march to Tunis, Travels in Morocco
s: has_destination Tunis The return march involved camps at Sheesheeah, Ghortabah, Ghafsa, Byrlafee, Sidi-Ben-Habeeba, Sidi-Mahammedeah, and Momakeeah before the party reached Tunis. The march was marked by abrupt changes from intense heat to freezing cold, difficult clay roads, strong winds, locusts, and the deaths or disappearance of many people and animals.

l: deaths from extreme weather, Travels in Morocco
s: On the march back to Tunis near Ghortabah, excessive heat killed two prisoners and one Turk. A sudden temperature fall then killed ten men, followed by eight burials, three missing men, and many dead camels and horses.

l: sea voyage from Mogador, Travels in Morocco
s: lasts one month [at sea and out of view of shore] After departing Mogador, the vessel soon lost sight of land and spent the next month at sea. The narrator remained in bed for twenty-five days, living on bread, water, and a little biscuit, while a horse and a young vulture died during the voyage; an aoudad survived and was later lodged in Regent’s Park.

l: gales at sea, Travels in Morocco
s: come_from north and north-east [successive gales of foul wind] The voyage encountered successive gales of foul wind from the north and northeast, with huge rising waves and foam. The schooner’s bows were repeatedly under water, and Captain Taylor sometimes rushed on deck to swear at the gale and sea.

The Renshaw schooner is a beautiful, fine-sailing, flat-bottomed shallow-draft vessel made for Barbary ports. After the narrator leaves the Governor at Mogador, it carries the narrator, a horse, young vulture, and an aoudad for Mr. Willshire and the Zoological Society through severe Atlantic weather.

l: French bombarding squadron, Travels in Morocco
s: French bombarding squadron comprising Gemappes, Suffren, Triton, Belle Poule, Asmodee, Pluton, and brigs; it silenced Mogador's batteries before French forces landed on the isle.

is_a English frigate The English frigate Warspite reached Mogador on 13 August. Its captain strongly remonstrated with the Moorish authorities but could not obtain permission for the British Consul, his wife, or other Europeans to leave.

l: wife of the British Consul, Travels in Morocco
s: is_detained_in Mogador [during the bombardment] The wife of the British Consul was refused permission to leave because Sidi Abdallah Deleero claimed that husband and wife were one. During the escape, she spoke Arabic to a marauding band and persuaded them not to kill her or her companions.

is_detained_in Mogador [during the bombardment] Mr. Robertson escaped with his wife and four children during the sack of Mogador. He narrowly avoided a sabre blow and reached the water-port after one of his daughters was threatened with a dagger for money.

is_detained_in Mogador [during the bombardment] Mrs. Robertson escaped with her infant and another child but became separated from Mr. Robertson in the crowd. She later rejoined him at the water-port in a fainting condition.
Mr. Lucas, rescuer of detained Europeans, builds a raft, reaches the French brig Canard for help, returns by boat, and arranges fugitives’ transfer to the Warspite.
defends isle of Mogador The Moorish garrison defended Mogador and the isle but was overcome by the French. About five hundred Moors were reported killed on the isle.
Wild tribes entered Mogador after authorities fled, sacking and burning it while attacking inhabitants, especially Jews and Europeans, with murder, assault, robbery, and violence.

l: Jews of Mogador, Travels in Morocco
s: The Jews of Mogador, especially those in the Jewish quarter, were exposed to assault, robbery, stripping, and murder during the sack. Poor Jews were maltreated, and many were left to accompany the natives in misery.

l: isle of Mogador, Travels in Morocco
s: has_parts Mogador forts and batteries Nine hundred French troops landed on the isle of Mogador on 16 August. After a rough encounter with the garrison, they captured the isle and its forts.

l: Mogador forts and batteries, Travels in Morocco
s: The Mogador forts and batteries were subjected to the French squadron's fire and were eventually silenced. The Moorish defenders abandoned them after the death of their best gunner.

The Mogador water-port served as the intended place of escape for the Consul's party and the Robertson family. Mr. Lucas reached it by boat after contacting the French fleet, and the fugitives were subsequently rescued from the area.

l: escape of the detained Europeans, Travels in Morocco
s: is_a escape [from the sack of Mogador] The detained Europeans escaped during the night through streets filled with fighting and plunder. The British Consul's party and the Robertson family endured attacks, while Mr. Lucas secured rescue by rafting to the French fleet.

l: commerce with Morocco, Travels in Morocco
s: has_part Tangier Commerce with Morocco included British and foreign imports of textiles, metals, dyes, foodstuffs, and manufactured goods in exchange for hides, wool, wax, almonds, fruit, grain, oil, and other produce. The unit gives commercial details for Tangier, Mogador, Rabat, and Mazagan and repeatedly attributes limited trade to high duties, monopolies, and restrictive fiscal laws.

has_part Mogador exports Mogador exported valuable Moroccan products and imported mainly Manchester cotton goods and other manufactured articles for local and inland consumption. Its trade increased because of strong demand for olive oil, and the text states that more liberal government would greatly expand commerce.
Mogador's exports included olive oil, almonds, gums, wool, seeds, skins, ostrich feathers, and occasional maize, valued in 1855 for British and foreign ports.

Mogador imports comprised British and foreign goods, including Manchester cottons, foodstuffs, metals, textiles, and mirrors; in 1855 British imports totaled L136,496 7s. 6d., with goods consumed inland to Timbuctoo.

is_rejected_by Moors [throughout Barbary] The text rejects the report that a beautiful young girl was sacrificed before the Sultan of Morocco, calling it an unmitigated libel. It states that human sacrifice is repudiated by every class in Barbary and is unknown to the Moors.

is_a mountain system [covering the heights of the Maghreb and elevations of the Sahara] The Atlantic System is the name Monsieur Balbi gives to the extensive mountain system of the Maghreb and the elevations scattered through the Sahara. Its principal ridge is said to extend from near Cape Noun on the Atlantic to east of the Great Syrte in Tripoli, with its greatest heights in Morocco.
